title: Short Stuff: Fortune Cookies
summary: Short Stuff episode on the origins of fortune cookies. The hosts debunk the idea that fortune cookies come from China, describing the Chinese moon cake legend (Mongol-era hidden messages, with the lotus paste and salted duck egg yolk filling) and the children's birth cake tradition as possible sources of the myth. They trace the likely origins to Japanese fortune crackers in Kyoto in the 1870s, then to the San Francisco Japanese Tea Garden caretaker Makoto Hagiwara around 1907, versus the Los Angeles claim involving David Jung of the Hong Kong Noodle Company. They cover the San Francisco mock court ruling, Japanese bakers dominating production until internment during World War Two, Chinese American bakers filling the gap, the shift to Americanized fortunes with lottery numbers and emoji, and the failed Wonton Food Company push into China.
topics: David Jung Hong Kong Noodle Company

entities.name: Court of Historical Reviews and Appeals

segments.title: Opening banter and fortune cookie basics
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the Short Stuff episode on fortune cookies and joke about their taste. They note that the fortune is not baked into the cookie but folded in after baking while still pliable. Off-topic chatter about an Atlanta Asian grocery store and egg rolls follows.

segments.title: Myth that fortune cookies come from China
segments.summary: The hosts say the belief that fortune cookies come from China is probably wrong. They describe moon cakes from the mid-Autumn festival, with lotus seed and red date pastes and salted duck egg yolks, and a legend that Chinese people hid messages in moon cakes during Mongol rule. They also mention the custom of sending cake rolls with messages to announce births.

segments.title: Japanese fortune crackers in Kyoto
segments.summary: The hosts say fortune cookies probably came from Japan and America. They describe fortune crackers in Kyoto from the 1870s, which were flavored with miso or sesame and had fortunes tucked into the fold rather than baked inside.

segments.title: Makoto Hagiwara and the San Francisco origin claim
segments.summary: The earliest American story dates to 1907 and involves Makoto Hagiwara, caretaker of the Japanese Tea Garden in Golden Gate Park. He was reportedly fired by the San Francisco mayor, then rehired after public support, and he gave out fortune cookies with thank-you notes.

segments.title: Los Angeles claim and San Francisco mock court
segments.summary: Los Angeles claims the fortune cookie was invented there by David Jung of the Hong Kong Noodle Company, who handed out cookies with Bible verses or as appetizers while people waited for tables. A San Francisco mock court, the Court of Historical Reviews and Appeals, ruled in favor of San Francisco. The hosts joke about the rivalry and a past show in San Diego.
topics: Court of Historical Reviews and Appeals

segments.title: Japanese bakers, internment, and Americanized fortunes
segments.summary: Japanese bakers in San Francisco dominated fortune cookie production until World War Two, when they were forced out after Pearl Harbor and interned. Chinese immigrants then filled the gap. Fortunes became more English and Americanized by the 1930s, adding Confucius sayings, almanac lines, lottery numbers, and emoji, which the hosts dislike.

segments.title: Wonton Food Company and the failed China market
segments.summary: In the mid-1990s the Wonton Food Company, described as the world's largest fortune cookie maker, tried to enter the Chinese market, but the cookies did not catch on there. The hosts note that the company makes about three billion cookies a year.

segments.title: Credits and sources
segments.summary: The hosts credit sources including What's Cooking America, LA Times Today History, and Jennifer 8 Lee's book The Fortune Cookie Chronicles, then sign off.
